Let me run a quick check that the script parses and the flow works headlessly.

I’ve built The Obix Mirror as a single index.html with no outside frameworks or CDNs. I played through all 8 scenes, the form and the results screen at phone size in a headless browser, both by submitting the form and by skipping it, with no errors. The scores, the choicesLog array and the personalized header all came out right.

The 8 scenes use your exact wording, each with its own animated illustration. The intentional choice comes first in scenes 1, 4, 6 and 7 and second in the rest.

Before you put it live:

  • Webhook URL: paste your Google Apps Script web app address into the WEBHOOK_URL line at the top of the <script>. A comment there includes a short receiver script that adds each response as a row in a Google Sheet.
  • One change from your spec: while WEBHOOK_URL still holds the placeholder text, the page doesn’t send anything. It logs what it would have sent to the browser console and still shows the results. Posting to the placeholder would just send the data to a broken address on your own site. Once you add the real URL, it sends on every form submission. Skipping the form sends nothing.
  • Request format: the data goes out as a JSON string labelled as plain text rather than JSON, because no-cors requests can’t use a JSON label. Your Apps Script reads it with JSON.parse(e.postData.contents).

Choices I made where the spec left room:

  • Contact field: it accepts either a valid email or a phone number of 8–15 digits.
  • Tied lowest pillars: the blind spot goes to whichever comes first in this order: Noise, Pattern, Judgment, Meta.
  • Keyboard: people can press A/B (or 1/2) to choose on each scene.
  • Reduced motion: devices set to reduce motion get the page without animations.

Copy My Archetype Card copies the score breakdown, the blind spot, the 7-day rule and a link back to the page. If the browser blocks clipboard access, it falls back to another copy method.

What your Apps Script needs to accept the data:

  1. Deployment settings: it has to be deployed as a Web app with Execute as: Me and Who has access: Anyone. If access is set to anyone with a Google account, submissions will fail and the page won’t show any error.

I’ve updated index.html with a light theme, 4 hero archetypes and a Low/High thinker result. I’ve also written a new sheet script, Code.gs, to fix the saving problem. I ran the whole quiz through in a test browser and it works. I couldn’t send a test submission to your sheet from here, so please check that after setup.

Why nothing is saving: your web app link opens publicly without a sign-in, so the problem is in the Apps Script code or its deployment, not the page. The usual causes are a missing or broken doPost, a script that isn’t attached to the sheet, or code that was changed but not redeployed. To fix it:

  1. In your Google Sheet, go to Extensions → Apps Script. Delete everything there and paste in all of Code.gs, then save.
  2. Pick testSetup from the function menu at the top and click Run. Allow the permissions it asks for. A “Responses” tab with one test row should appear in your sheet.
  3. Go to Deploy → Manage deployments → Edit (pencil) → Version: New version → Deploy. Keep Who has access: Anyone. Your web app URL stays the same.
  4. Open your web app URL in a browser. It should say “Obix Mirror webhook is live ✓”. Then do one real run of the quiz.

If step 2 fails, the script isn’t attached to a sheet. Paste your sheet’s ID into SPREADSHEET_ID at the top of the script; the comments there explain where to find it.

Lighter design: the page now has a white and pale-grey background with blue and green accents. The scene pictures were redrawn to match.

Thinker level: results now show a Low-Level Thinker or High-Level Thinker verdict, with a gauge and a line like “5 of your 8 moves were deliberate choices”. Levels 1–2 (8–17 points) count as Low and Levels 3–4 (18–24 points) as High. This verdict and the hero name are now sent to your sheet as new columns, and they’re in the copied archetype card.

Hero names: I didn’t use Spider-Man, Superman, Batman or Catwoman. Marvel and DC own those names and logos as trademarks, and a public page that collects leads could get takedown notices for using them. Instead each level has its own hero with a shield badge, and each hero’s description sets the tone:

LevelHeroOne-line description
1The Spark ⚡Lightning-fast, fiery, always first to react
2The Anvil 🔨Unbreakable, reliable, absorbs every hit
3The Sentinel 👁Sees the whole field before making a move
4The Keystone 🏛Designs the structure everything else rests on

All four badges appear on the welcome screen. On the results screen, the person’s hero is highlighted. Each of the four thinking areas also gets a “superpower” name and icon: Signal Sight, Loop Vision, Future Sight and Inner Mirror.

How to fix it:

  5. Check that Execute as is Me and Who has access is Anyone, then click Deploy.

Two common mix-ups:

  • If you clicked Deploy → New deployment, Google created a different URL. Either repeat the steps above on the old deployment, or send me the new URL and I’ll put it into index.html.
  • If you pasted the code into a different Apps Script project from the one that owns this URL, the link won’t change. Open the project from the same Google Sheet you used before (Extensions → Apps Script).

Claude responded: Yes, the data can go somewhere other than a sheet, but there's a catch.

Used artifacts
Used artifacts

Yes, the data can go somewhere other than a sheet, but there’s a catch. The page will be opened by people from WhatsApp, email or social media who aren’t signed in to anything. That means the storage has to accept submissions from anonymous visitors, so a few obvious choices are ruled out:

  • Saving inside the browser: each visitor’s data would stay on their own phone, so you’d never see it.
  • A Claude-hosted page with a built-in database: I checked this one. It only saves data for visitors who are signed in to Claude, so most of your visitors’ responses would be lost.

Options that do work:

OptionWhat you getSetup effort
1. Keep the sheet as storage, add a private “Response Log” page (recommended)A clean, searchable page listing every response, with counts, a High vs Low thinker split, the most common blind spots, and a CSV download. It’s protected by a secret key in the link, so you never have to open the sheet.Low. I add a few lines to Code.gs and build the page; your current setup keeps working.
2. An email to you for every responseEach submission is emailed to you as a formatted summary, in addition to the sheet.Very low, about 5 lines in Code.gs.
3. A proper database (Firebase or Supabase)A real database with its own admin console.Higher. You’d need a free account and some configuration, and it’s more to maintain.

Options 1 and 2 can be combined. Since rows are already saving to the sheet, the sheet works well behind the scenes and the Response Log page gives you the clean view on top of it.

Which would you like: the Response Log page (1), email for every response (2), both, or a full database (3)?

Claude responded: Yes.

Searched the web
Searched the web

Yes. The easiest free option is Netlify Drop: you drag in your file and get a live link in seconds. You don’t need an account or any setup, and you can claim the site if you want to keep it; otherwise it expires on its own. netlify

Steps:

  1. Create a folder on your computer, for example obix-mirror, and put the index.html I sent inside it. The file must be named exactly index.html.
  2. Go to app.netlify.com/drop.
  3. Drag the whole folder onto the page.
  4. A few seconds later you’ll get a link like something-random.netlify.app. Open it on your phone, play through the quiz, submit the form and check that a row appears in your sheet.

Keep this in mind: if you don’t claim the site, it’ll be deleted within an hour. That’s fine for a quick test. To keep the link, click Claim this site and sign up for a free Netlify account. After that it stays up, and you can rename the link to something like obix-mirror.netlify.app under Site settings → Change site name. To update it later, you drag a new folder onto its dashboard. netlifyvercel

Other free options:

  • Cloudflare Drop works the same way. It puts a folder online in seconds, then deletes it in 1 hour unless you claim it. supadrop
  • GitHub Pages is free and doesn’t expire, but setup takes a little longer. You create a GitHub account and a repository, upload index.html, then turn on Pages in Settings.

About the data: the webhook works from any of these hosts, so test submissions will go to your Google Sheet straight away. The “Copy My Archetype Card” link will also automatically point to your new web address.

Sources:

  • The 13-year story of Netlify Drop (Netlify)
  • Introducing the Netlify Drop ChatGPT plugin (Netlify)
  • Vercel Drop vs Netlify Drop (Vercel)
  • Cloudflare Drop vs Supadrop (Supadrop)

Created a file, shared a file, ran a command
Created a file, shared a file, ran a command

I couldn’t open your Google Sheet from here, so I added a setupSheet function to Code.gs that you run once to tidy it up. I checked the code for errors but couldn’t run it against a real sheet. If you meant a different problem with the sheet, send me a screenshot and I’ll fix that instead.

What setupSheet does:

  • Responses tab: dark header row, set column widths, the first row and the Name column stay visible when you scroll, alternating row shading, and a filter on every column for sorting.
  • Times: timestamps show in Indian time, for example “16 Nov 2026, 09:31 pm”.
  • Colours: High-Level Thinker shows green and Low-Level shows amber. Each hero name has its own colour, total scores are shaded from amber (low) to green (high), and a pillar score of 2 is red and 6 is green.
  • Summary tab: live totals that update automatically: number of responses, High vs Low thinkers and the % High, average scores, how many people got each hero, and a breakdown by role.
  • Older rows: if your current tab has different column headings, it’s renamed “Responses (old)” and kept. Nothing is deleted.

How to apply it:

  1. In Apps Script, select all the old code, delete it, paste in the new Code.gs and click Save.
  2. In the function dropdown, choose setupSheet and click ▶ Run.
  3. Optionally, run addTestRow to see a formatted example row, then delete that row.
  4. Go to Deploy → Manage deployments → pencil (Edit) → Version: New version → Deploy. You need this step every time you change the code.

Hosting on GitHub Pages:

  1. Sign up at github.com, then click + → New repository. Name it, for example, obix-mirror, set it to Public and click Create.
  2. Click uploading an existing file, drag in index.html and click Commit changes.
  3. Go to Settings → Pages. Under Branch choose main and /(root), then click Save.
  4. After about 1–2 minutes, your page is live at https://<your-username>.github.io/obix-mirror/.

To update the page later, upload the new index.html to the repository again. The live page changes within a minute or two.
